claims.text: A uniformly alloyed steel microstructure promotes formation of a continuous, stable passive oxide film.
A uniformly alloyed microstructure enhances recombination of irradiation-induced defects.
The combination of passive-film uniformity and enhanced defect recombination reduces localized galvanic cells.
The proposed synergy limits the initiation and propagation of corrosion.
Baseline steels normally exhibit micro-heterogeneities in Cu, Cr, and Ni.
Elemental segregation in baseline steel leads to nonuniform passive-film formation.
Lowering Cu and optimizing Cr can suppress segregation in the proposed steel.
The proposed alloy adjustment can preserve mechanical and corrosion-resistant properties while suppressing segregation.
Uniform dispersion of alloying elements minimizes secondary-phase segregation.
Microstructural heterogeneities are prone to act as localized-corrosion initiation sites.
A more uniform passive oxide film is more resistant to breakdown under harsh aqueous and irradiation conditions.
An even distribution of alloying elements facilitates greater recombination of irradiation-induced vacancies and interstitials.
Greater irradiation-defect recombination limits defect accumulation.
Compositionally uniform steels will have lower corrosion rates and lower polarization current densities than segregated baseline steels.
Compositionally uniform steels will accumulate fewer irradiation-induced defects than segregated baseline steels.
The predicted improvements should occur in both standard electrochemical tests and simulated irradiation conditions.
The mechanism should hold in moderately aggressive aqueous environments and at irradiation levels typical of chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
The mechanism may cease to apply outside the studied environmental conditions or compositional ranges.
